KZN Oncology/Urology Updated [5173]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Production

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
KZN Report Card Proposal

In July last year Carte Blanche broadcast a programme on the oncology crisis in KZN. The greater Durban area’s last oncologist resigned. The South African Human Rights Commission wrote a damning report about the situation.

Six months later nothing has changed. There are still no oncologists in Durban, the radiotherapy machines are still not working and thousands of patients are unable to get the medical care they deserve.

On the weekend the Department of Health says they do have a plan to address the crisis which involves getting doctors from India and Cuba.
They assure the public that the radiography machines will be fixed by April

Many people who work in the field believe that the Department of Health will not be able to deliver on the promises. There are still human rights abuses as parents are not able to access the care that they need.
And then the last urologist left State Employ. A case study was given a date of an operation in 2024 to address her issues around her bladder.

Here is a list of people we would need to interview.
KZN Oncology Crisis

1. Sphelele from CANSA. PMB
Staff members have faced PTSD as they have not been able to help people coming to them for help with collapse of health care services.
2. Imran Keeka. Approached the SAHRC to formulate report about Human Right’s Abuses against people who cannot access health care. PMB Part of DA but he has been the driver behind uncovering the crisis is KZN.
3. Geraldine from past programme who was incorrectly diagnosed and due to selling their car managed to get proper health care and now cancer free.
4. Grey’s Hospital link.
5. Addington Hospital Link Requested interviews but declined.
6. Varian manufacturers of machines have asked for a statement.
7. SAHRC statement. Link to say requested interview and delaying.
8. Bernie Van Heerden 0621343019 Urology patient. Problems in May last year.Went to Port Shepstone. Told that there was a problem with prostrate. Private doctor tested him for nothing his PSA cound was 113, meant to be 4. Prescribed premerin. Shepstone gave him drug for one month and then put him on injections brought count down to 8. He has to have a biopsy. First told at Addington that he could have it in 2021. Daughter phoned all over got him appointment in 15 February. Does not know what happens next. What he has to do etc.
9. Dr Musa Gumede Acting HOD of Health – requested interview. Waiting for a response.
10. Christo. Mother has prolapsed bladder appointment in 2024. They will talk to us.
11. Visuals of Greys, Addington, Albert Lithuli
12. Dr Mzukwa Chairman of SAMA in KZN. Available for an interview – waiting to confirm urology case study.
He has case study for us.

Still to contact case study Malaleveva Majola 084 2226858

Natasha was diagnosed with stage one cancer in December but has quickly progressed to stage 3, due to the backlog Greys Hospital can only see her in April.

New plan to address issues. https://www.timeslive.co.za/news/south-africa/2018-01-30-cuban-and-indian-doctors-to-solve-kzn-oncology-crisis/

Press Release:


KZN Oncology Crisis
In June last year, the South African Human Rights Commission gave the KwaZulu-Natal Health department binding recommendations to improve oncology services in the province. But seven months later, despite promises by Health MEC Dr Sibongiseni Dhlomo that a number of machines would function by January 2018, many are still not working. There are still no oncologists available and thousands of State cancer patients continue languishing in regional hospitals waiting for medical assistance. The backlog is immense and the prognosis is dire.


Script:


Oncology Script


V/O
The KZN state oncology crisis is critical
and thousands of people are not getting the help they desperately need.

Claire
“If I was diagnosed with cancer in KZN…”


Claire
“….will I die?”

Dr Mzukwa
“Definitely because there is no oncologist to see you or treat you.”

V/O
Dr Mvuyisi Mzukwa is a private doctor in Isipingo Hills, South of Durban and he has seen many of his patients die because they can not access cancer treatment.


Zodwa is one of his patients and one of many KZN victims for whom time is running out.
She has stage 4 cervical cancer and is being treated at the Prince Mshiyeni Memorial Hospital.
She is cared for, but there is no one there to treat her.
She lives in Umlazi, with her mother, Zanele, who asked us to hide her face.
She doesn’t want anything to jeopardise her daughter’s chances of getting help.

“Zanele”
“They havent told us anything about when they are going to start the chemo. They said that they don’t deal with cancer – Albert Lithuli does, which means that they are just a waiting room.”

V/O
We accompanied Ma Zanele on a hospital visit. Zodwa became ill in 2015, but local clinics could find nothing wrong with her. When she met Dr Mzukwa he said she had cancer symptoms. He pressurised the authorities at Prince Mshiyeni Hospital to treat her immediately. But there is such a huge backlog of cancer patients waiting for help.

Zodwa
“The doctor said that the hospital can’t tell a patient who has cancer in January 2018, that they can only receive treatment in 2019.”

Zodwa
“I am scared when I see people dying around me. When I see them die, I fear that I am going to follow them.”


Zanele
“If I am not mistaken five people have died since she’s been there. “

Dr Mzukwa
“I mean it is psychologically traumatising to see patients who are waiting to be treated for cancerous lesions to be dying in front of you. It tells you that your turn is coming”

V/O

Prayer is all these families have.

Up sound

V/O
In July last year Carte Blanche highlighted this issue when the last state oncologist in the Durban area resigned.

The South African Human Rights Commission released a damning report, condemning the KZN Health Department on these human rights abuses against oncology patients.
Their CEO Tseliso Thipanyane was spear heading the investigation.

Devi
“In the end this is a matter of life and death”

Tseliso
“This is a matter of life and death that's why we are asking the department to tell us how many patients have died because of their inability to do their jobs.”

V/ O
It’s not only a lack of oncologists but a lack of working radiotherapy machines.

Link
There are two radiotherapy machines here at Addington Hospital, when we came here last July they weren’t working and even after promises from the KZN MEC Dr Dhlomo that they would be fixed. 7 months down the line nothing has changed and they are still not operational.

V/O
In fact, they haven’t worked for nearly 5 years.

“The oncology crisis in KZN whose fault is it?”
The point of your fault is it lies with the person who never fixed our machines.
Are you passing the buck MEC?
I don’t fix machines, I don’t
But you are responsible and the MEC for Health
That is why you and I will have a different viewpoint on this matter.”



V/O
Apart from broken machines at Addington,
Grey’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg has the only working cancer unit with 4 oncologists and 1 working machine.
At Inkosi Albert Luthuli Hospital there are 3 working machines, but no oncologists.
A nurse from the hospital agreed to speak to us only if we could hide her identity.

“Could you tell me know what the situation is in oncology?”

Sue
16 secs 20 frames
Right now there is a crisis in oncology, there are no oncologists. Patients are being turned away on a daily basis. There is a huge backlog in the department. Machines are working in radiation but there are no doctors to see patients to plan their treatment.”


Claire link
“In KZN if you are diagnosed with cancer the chances of getting treatment timeously are slim many desperate patients try to get the help they need by travelling to other provinces.

V/O
Lorraine Govender is from the Cancer Association of South Africa.

Lorraine
“In the last two years we have had an influx of complaints of the public raising concerns that they can’t access cancer treatment in KZN and we have had success stories of patients who have gone to Pretoria and Western Cape and had treatment successfully.”

V/O
CANSA provides support to everyone diagnosed with cancer.
Siphelelisiwe Mabaso says she really struggles emotionally when the state system doesn’t allow her to help patients. This is an sms she received.

Claire
“Sometimes you have to deal with heart breaking situations?”

Sphe
“So this was a message that I received Claire from the last patient, which I have worked with.And she said,”I need drastic and urgent help, and the only time that they can help me at Grey’s Hospital is on the 24th of April. I can’t wait that long. I feel sick and I am in pain, and I need them to take out whatever it is that they need to, as soon as possible.I am devastated, scared and I need urgent help.”

Claire
“When was that sent and what happened?”

Sphe
“This was sent on the 23rd of January and the patient passed on the 5th of Feb.”

Claire
“How does it affect you?”

Sphe
“Like I said, it actually has come to a point where sometimes I don’t even want to meet these patients. Cause I could tell from the advances of her cancer hat it is very aggressive and she probably would not be able to make it.”

V/O
KZN’s DA Health spokesman Dr Imran Keeka said he first approached the SAHRC to investigate these human rights abuses.

Claire
“Do we have any idea how many lives have been lost due to this crisis?”

Imran
“The Health MEC Dr Dlhomo and Dr Motswaldi the national health minister deny that they know the exact numbers however I do have a response to parliamentary question bearing the MEC’s signature that says in the year 2015/16, 459 patients died as a result of the oncology crisis and that’s only at 1 facility, at Inkosi Albert Luthuli Hospital.

V/O

To put it in perspective, if 459 people held hands they could circle the circumference of a rugby field twice.

V/O
We took a hidden camera to see what the situation was like at Albert Luthuli. In the oncology department we found a room full of patients, waiting for the oncologist. Most of these appointments were scheduled up to 6 months ago.

“Are there any oncologists here today?”
“We actually don’t know what’s going on”

V/O
Sue says that this happens daily.
7 secs 20 frames
“They take down the names and telephone numbers of the patients and they get told that when an oncologist arrives, the patients will be called.”

Up sound write names down

“Is anyone called back?”
3sec 14
“No, there’s no doctors, so we haven’t called any patients.”
“So what do they do?”
9 secs 21 f
“If you have got medical aid, well and good you can go to private. But if you don’t have medical aid unfortunately you will go home and die.”

Claire Link
We requested an interview with the Department’s acting head Dr Musa Gumede and he declined.
V/O
The MEC Dr Sibongiseni Dhlomo also declined,
Citing ongoing negotiations with stakeholders.

V/O
Dr Dhlomo has been criticized for mismanagement and a lack of accountability . We however caught up with him on a personal press junket, visiting Inkosi Albert Luthuli hospital. He wanted selected media to know of his plans to bring 3 oncologists here from the Wits Health Consortium.

While he was happy to have photographs taken with the cancer machines, he avoided cancer patients waiting in the Oncology Department for doctors who never arrive.

Sue
7 secs 13 frames
“I think it’s very important for the viewers to know that that we feel let down by the powers that be, including management and the MEC.

Imran Keeka
“He made a pubic statement recently to say that there are 3 machines at IALH and that are oncologists are there daily and I cant be more blunt to say that that is a lie.”

V/O
Last year doctors and nurses marched in Durban to highlight the collapse of the KZN healthcare system. Dr Mzukwa says oncologists left because they were frustrated with not being able to treat patients effectively because of broken equipment.

Dr Mzukwa
“The morale is very low because I don’t think it’s a good thing to see patients dying when you know what it is that should be done for those patients. And you know that the department is capable of doing this service for the patient but they are just dragging their feet and they just don’t care.”

V/O
Dr Keeka is sceptical of Dr Dhlomo’s plans.

“You can’t say that there is no money to fix equipment because it says that there will be under expenditure of machinery and equipment and it gives an amount of the region of 50 million.”

Claire
“How is that possible?”

Imran
“Now that is the thing. You telling us you don’t have the money to buy a radiotherapy machine when the figures tell us that you do but you have taken that money from there to use for something else. Where are the priorities?”

V/O
Zodwa has been in hospital for 3 weeks now, her condition is deteriorating and she still hasn’t seen an oncologist.

Zodwa
“I don’t think he (the MEC) cares about people in government hospitals. They don’t get any help.

“I think patients need to know that they have a right to health care, everyone needs to have access to treatment, it’s a privilege and right.”

Studio Outro

Although Dr Dhlomo said that there would be oncologists working at Inkhosi Albert Lithuli by the 15th of February, they are still waiting for them to come.



Promo 1 x 15 secs

V/O
The Kzn state oncology crisis is critical and thousands of people are not getting the help they desperately need.

If I get cancer in KZN will I die?
Definitely because there is no oncologist.



Promo 2
“At Inkhosi Albert Lithuli Hospital in the last two weeks there has been nobody to see patients for chemotherapy All the patients have been turned away.”

How many more people have to die before KZN Health allows cancer patients the right to medical care.

“Cancer does not wait.”

Promo 3 x 10 secs

Zodwa has stage 4 cancer and fears that she may die. KZN oncology is in crisis as cancer patients continue to wait for medical treatment they so desperately need.

Dr Mzukwa says oncologists left because they were frustrated with not being able to treat patients effectively because of broken equipment. Dr Mzukwa “The morale is very low because I don’t think it’s a good thing to see patients dying when you know what it is that should be done for those patients. And you know that the department is capable of doing this service for the patient but they are just dragging their feet and they just don’t care.” V/O Dr Keeka is sceptical of Dr Dhlomo’s plans. “You can’t say that there is no money to fix equipment because it says that there will be under expenditure of machinery and equipment and it gives an amount of the region of 50 million.” Claire “How is that possible?” Imran “Now that is the thing. You telling us you don’t have the money to buy a radiotherapy machine when the figures tell us that you do but you have taken that money from there to use for something else. Where are the priorities?” V/O Zodwa has been in hospital for 3 weeks now, her condition is deteriorating and she still hasn’t seen an oncologist. Zodwa “I don’t think he (the MEC) cares about people in government hospitals. They don’t get any help. “I think patients need to know that they have a right to health care, everyone needs to have access to treatment, it’s a privilege and right.” Studio Outro Although Dr Dhlomo said that there would be oncologists working at Inkhosi Albert Lithuli by the 15th of February, they are still waiting for them to come. Promo 1 x 15 secs V/O The Kzn state oncology crisis is critical and thousands of people are not getting the help they desperately need. If I get cancer in KZN will I die? Definitely because there is no oncologist. Promo 2 “At Inkhosi Albert Lithuli Hospital in the last two weeks there has been nobody to see patients for chemotherapy All the patients have been turned away.” How many more people have to die before KZN Health allows cancer patients the right to medical care. “Cancer does not wait.” Promo 3 x 10 secs Zodwa has stage 4 cancer and fears that she may die. KZN oncology is in crisis as cancer patients continue to wait for medical treatment they so desperately need.

metadata.Further information: KZN Report Card Proposal In July last year Carte Blanche broadcast a programme on the oncology crisis in KZN. The greater Durban area’s last oncologist resigned. The South African Human Rights Commission wrote a damning report about the situation. Six months later nothing has changed. There are still no oncologists in Durban, the radiotherapy machines are still not working and thousands of patients are unable to get the medical care they deserve. On the weekend the Department of Health says they do have a plan to address the crisis which involves getting doctors from India and Cuba. They assure the public that the radiography machines will be fixed by April Many people who work in the field believe that the Department of Health will not be able to deliver on the promises.
